Business.title: How I beat my late-night shopping addiction
Business.text:
You may well have been there. It's late, you're scrolling on your phone and suddenly feel a strong urge to buy something - only to wake up the next day and regret it.

But what happens when those impulse buys become a habit rather than a one-off?

One global study suggests 7% of adults, external experience shopping addiction, external - an uncontrollable urge to spend despite the financial consequences - and younger women are more susceptible.

Ella Hewitt, from Liverpool, says her shopping addiction got so bad in 2021 that she was spending up to £700 a month on fast fashion she couldn't afford and sometimes never even wore.

"I didn't grow up with much money, so when I got a job I would spend my wages as soon as they hit my account," says the 24-year-old.

"That dopamine hit kept me shopping and in the world of social media there is just so much encouragement to do that."

She says she would often make purchases on TikTok or Instagram when she was "tired" or "bored", lured by the latest trends on her feeds.

She was working as an HR assistant in a school at the time and her spending meant she couldn't afford to move out of her family home.

"Horrified" by how much she was buying, she began using diversionary tactics to control her spending.

One was to put anything she felt like buying on a wish list and wait 30 days.

"If I still wanted it, I would buy it, but more often than not I'd find the urge had gone," she says.

Ella gave herself an imaginary budget of £1,000 each day to spend on imaginary purchases, which "scratched the itch" of shopping without the cost.

And she vowed only to buy something if she could afford to "buy it three times".

"Overall, I cut my spending by about 60%," says Ella, who now works as an ethical fashion influencer and plans to launch her own clothing brand.

"I'm not perfect. There are times when I will buy things because I want it. But I am way more in control."

Research last year from Vanquis, a challenger bank, found Gen Z shoppers make more impulse purchases than any other age group, external, closely followed by millennials.

And some experts say exposure to social media, with its targeted advertising, influencer culture and seamless one-click checkout, is fuelling the trend, external.

Money and Mental Health, a charity, also blames the design of online shopping sites for "minimising the friction around spending money".

It points to "pop-ups" that put customers under pressure to spend, and the inclusion of alternative payment methods like Buy Now Pay Later.

The BBC has contacted Meta, which owns Instagram, TikTok and Asos for comment.

Business.title: Military veterans told they owe thousands of pounds over clerical error
Business.text:
Hundreds of former members of the military have had their pensions slashed after receiving letters telling them to repay thousands of pounds because of a clerical error.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) confirmed to the BBC that more than 1000 retired service personnel are being pursued for debts. The majority, 335 veterans, were overpaid a total of £5.1m as a result of incorrect National Insurance calculations.

The Forces Pension Society said it is aware of a small number of veterans whose debts were wiped after raising a formal complaint.

Ray Lawton, 70, was told in July he owed £8,000 following six years of overpayments. Days later, his monthly military pension was cut from £550 to £365.

"I haven't got £8,000 to pay out," said Lawton, who served 16 years in the Royal Artillery.

"I've got a little bit put aside but nowhere near that much."

The Portsmouth-based veteran told the BBC: "I've trusted the army all my life even when I left and I trusted my pension would be right. Then this letter comes and it's just blown it all out."

Lawton's letter was sent from a company called Equiniti, which administers the pension scheme on behalf of the MoD.

It said an error in its system meant he had been overpaid for years.

Lawton is one of many veterans from across the UK who contacted BBC Your Voice after receiving letters out of the blue seeking money they didn't know they owed.

The Forces Pension Society, a not-for-profit which supports military retirees, said it is aware of many overpayment cases running into the tens of thousands of pounds.

A small number of veterans have been told they owe six-figure sums.

The MoD confirmed errors relating to National Insurance adjustments, Pension Sharing Orders (PSO), Early Departure Payments (EDP) and State Pension Age (SPA). It says it is investigating issues on a case-by-case basis.

It added that of the 335 veterans affected by National Insurance errors, a third have paid off their debt in full and 52 have an agreed repayment plan in place. So far, of the £5.1m, £304,000 has been paid back.

Veterans said they want more clarity about the debt and how it has been calculated. Some have called for it to be wiped.

The government said it has a responsibility to recover the funds.

An MoD spokesperson told the BBC that it recognises that errors to pension payments "may cause uncertainty", adding that it is contacting veterans and "providing support for anyone who requires it".

"Where payments have been made in genuine error, we have a responsibility to recover taxpayer funds and will always seek to do so in a sensitive and proportionate way," the spokesperson added.

However, former Conservative defence secretary Penny Mordaunt, said: "While public bodies have a duty to recoup such costs if it makes financial sense to do so, no such assessment has been made in these cases.

"There is a compelling case in many instances for the debt to be wiped".

RAF veteran Barrie Goodwin contacted Equiniti six years ago after receiving a higher payment than he was expecting.

He was told the change was because he had reached state pension age. He's since been notified he was overpaid £32,188 and must hand it back.

"I checked, was told it was all correct and now have to repay it," he said. "I'm already cutting back on luxuries. I was helping one of my grandchildren through nursery - that's had to change.

"If the debt isn't waived, I will really struggle."

Equiniti told the BBC it could not discuss individual cases but recognised the concern caused to pensioners.

A spokesperson said it was not responsible for the decision to recoup taxpayers' money but "administration of a scheme of this scale involves multiple organisations, systems and processes over many years".

Technology company Sopra Steria has been in charge of the veterans' pension scheme since 2023, and had subcontracted the administration to Equiniti.

A Sopra Steria spokesperson told the BBC that "errors that led to incorrect pension payments originated over a decade before Sopra Steria took over the contract".

The company said it is "working closely with the MoD and Equiniti to ensure robust safeguards are in place for the long term".

The Forces Pension Society is advising anyone who receives an overpayment letter to verify its authenticity, request more information from Equiniti and using the right to complain through the Internal Disputes Procedure.

Additional reporting: Adam Clarkson and Elaine Doran

Business.title: Gatwick Airport facing water outage after main burst in Horley
Business.text:
Gatwick Airport passengers were left without water after a main burst in a nearby field.

SES Water said that it located a burst main in Horley, with parts of the airport left without water as a result.

A spokesperson for the airport confirmed that the issue had affected water supply in both terminals and was under investigation by SES Water. The water company said it had begun to restore supply and that water pressure was beginning to return to normal.

Flights remained unaffected by the disruption, the airport added.

The issues come after a major supply outage in July saw passengers face long queues for toilets at the West Sussex airport, with restaurants and bars also closing.

Natasha Nzekwe, who was due to fly to Amsterdam from the North Terminal, said: "It's quite frustrating, but everyone seems to be pretty fine.

"There's no water at all, you can't even wash your hands in the toilets.

"If I were on a long haul flight I think it would be worse, not being able to properly wash your hands is frustrating, and they haven't given us any information as to what is going on."

Naduni Abeywickrama, who was travelling from London to Aberdeen, added that the delay was "extremely frustrating".

She added: "No one seems to be making a scene, but I feel frustrated because this is the second time this has happened."

Toilets in the airport's North Terminal are closed as a result of the supply issue, while the majority of toilets in the South Terminal are unaffected.

Business.title: 'Cowboy builders' targeted in new government clampdown
Business.text:
People carrying out home renovations will gain greater protections against "cowboy builders" through a new database of trusted traders and a payment system offering more safeguards, the government has said.

Traders signing up to the scheme launching next month will need to demonstrate certain standards of customer service, transparency and dispute resolution.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unscrupulous tradespeople "leave families with months of stress" as well as unfinished work.

The National Federation of Builders said the changes would not stop rogue operators while the Tories suggested there would be added paperwork for firms already operating legitimately.

Citizens Advice has said home renovations are one of its biggest sources of consumer complaints.

The government said more than a quarter of people who carried out home improvements in the past 18 months have experienced problems, such as builders disappearing after upfront payments were made.

It cited a survey carried out for the Competition and Markets Authority, external suggesting customers lost more £10bn in 2024 on home and garden maintenance services due to losses, overpriced costs or unfair practices by traders.

BBC News has previously reported on "bait-and-switch" locksmith scams, where customers were given an initial cheap quote before hidden charges and unnecessary work were added.

Under the new traders' scheme, customers' money will be held in an account and released in parts after certain milestones in projects are completed.

The National Federation of Builders (NFB) told BBC Breakfast there are already schemes in place to find trustworthy builders.

Adas Rico Wojtulewicz-Richmond, the NFB's director of policy, said: "Is this scheme going to stop bad actors operating and ripping people off? I don't think it will."

He said a better approach would be for every project to have a "passport" which records all the work done.

"It protects consumers because you can find out which companies are doing a poor job, and it brings up the industry standards," he said.

The Chartered Trading Standards Institute (CTSI) said the new scheme would clamp down on rogue traders "who take the money and run", but urged the government to go further to protect vulnerable people from shoddy works and repairs.

John Herriman, CTSI's chief executive, said government funding schemes like the Warm Homes Plan, external could create opportunities for fraudulent traders.

"CTSI would therefore urge the government to see this as a great first step and to introduce a mandatory licence for tradespeople working in the home repair and maintenance sector, which would make it simpler and cheaper for enforcement agencies – including Trading Standards – to prosecute fraudulent tradespeople," he said.

BBC News has previously reported on botched insulation jobs carried out through government schemes since 2022.

Major defects have been found in over 30,000 houses linked to the schemes.

The prime minister said rogue tradespeople gave their "decent, hardworking" counterparts a bad name and would be "putting the cowboys out of business".

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said that, while home improvements can be stressful, "we're taking action to protect consumers, support reputable traders and make sure people can spend their money with greater confidence and security".

Shadow business secretary Andrew Griffith said the announcement looks like "the sort of government initiative that risks the unintended consequence of piling more paperwork onto the majority of businesses who already do the right thing".

He said: "The government would do far better to beef up law enforcement and have tougher sentences for the minority who fraudulently rip off customers. Those who break the rules will keep breaking them regardless of whether there is an app in the way."

Liberal Democrat business spokesperson Sarah Olney said: "Rogue builders cause real harm and ruin real lives every year. The current system is simply not fit for purpose and this half-baked announcement falls frustratingly short from fixing it.

"A voluntary code for tradespeople completely misses the mark. Rogue operators won't voluntarily sign up - they will simply keep exploiting families in the shadows."

Alongside action on rogue tradespeople, the government has announced plans to regulate private bailiffs in England and Wales, to protect people in debt from "intimidating behaviour, unfair treatment or being pushed into excessive repayment arrangements".

Under the changes, people facing enforcement action will have access to an independent complaints process, and private bailiffs will be held to professional standards.

Sarah Sackman, minister for courts and legal services, said bailiffs did an important job, but "with that responsibility must come high standards".

As part of the changes, the government will look at how organisations such as Trading Standards work with regulators and enforcement bodies "so consumers are not passed from pillar to post".

Last year, a Freedom of Information request by Which? revealed that understaffing in trading standards teams was leading to more scams and dangerous products being sold.

Business.title: AI build out: AI gold rush draws crypto firms away from Bitcoin
Business.text:
Companies that once filled warehouses with computers to earn Bitcoin - a process known as mining - are now using that computing power for AI.

Bitcoin mining companies invested large sums on giant banks of powerful computers as the price of Bitcoin rocketed in recent years.

But those mining companies have faced falling rewards since the value of the cryptocurrency has slumped from its peak in October 2025.

Now many are pivoting to AI and signing deals with companies such as Anthropic - who are spending billions of dollars on the infrastructure needed to keep up in the AI race.

Like AI systems, Bitcoin relies on vast networks of powerful computers housed in data centres.

Because Bitcoin operates without a central authority, these computers verify transactions and are rewarded with newly-created digital coins.

But the rewards have reduced and the value of coins has dropped since last year.

One bitcoin was worth about $124,000 (£91,000) at its peak in October 2025, but has since fallen sharply.

More recently, it has rallied to around $80,000 - meaning it is up almost 30% so far in August.

But, for companies that have already made the change, even that may not be enough to get them to return to the crypto industry, because the switch of use - once made - is expensive to undo.

Industry analysts say Bitcoin mining companies have been pivoting to AI because they have years of experience in finding cheap electricity and efficiently running large data centres.

TerraWulf, Ionic Digital, Core Scientific, Iris Energy, Bitdeer, Riot Platforms and Hut 8 are just some of the companies increasingly diverting investment and infrastructure from bitcoin mining towards AI.

Riot Platforms signed a $9bn, 20-year compute deal with Anthropic earlier this month.

Company names and websites are changing to reflect the shift too.

Applied Blockchain has become Applied Digital.

TerraWulf's website once described the firm as an "infrastructure-focused bitcoin mining company".

It now says it focuses on "next-generation AI and high-performance computing".

Enegix, which opened a huge Bitcoin mining site in Kazakhstan to great fanfare in 2020, is now pivoting too.

"Today, we are moving confidently towards artificial intelligence and planning the gradual alignment of our energy and infrastructure capabilities, both in Kazakhstan and elsewhere, towards the development of AI infrastructure," said the company's chief executive Yerbolsyn Sarsenov.

Enegix says it is in active discussions with AI and HPC (high-performance computing) companies and planning to transform a "significant" portion of the business to AI.

But refitting crypto mines for AI is expensive and in some cases the companies have had to sell some of their Bitcoin holdings to fund the switch.

Wolfie Zhao from The Energy Mag - a publication that rebranded from The Miner Mag to reflect the trend - predicts the industry pivot will continue even as the price of Bitcoin has risen in recent days.

"We expect to see many public miners continue winding down their Bitcoin mining hardware in the coming quarters," he said.

Asked if the shift away from Bitcoin mining might affect the security or stability of the cryptocurrency, Zhao said he hoped more miners will enter the market as conditions improve.

But he predicted many of the big players would not easily be able to switch back to Bitcoin.

"Once that multi-gigawatt power infrastructure has been retrofitted to AI or HPC colocation, there is no turning back," he said.

"You can unplug from the Bitcoin network any time but signing a GPU colocation lease for 10 or 20 years means steady revenue and a commitment to keep the infrastructure up for the tenants."

Bitdeer, which is one of the largest Bitcoin miners in the world, just announced a 16-year deal to provide compute for Anthropic.

But the company's chief strategy officer, Haris Basit, said Bitdeer will continue mining Bitcoin, believing many operators would ultimately pursue a dual-purpose model.

"Bitcoin mining is particularly well suited to that model because it is flexible and interruptible, while AI workloads can provide longer-duration contracted revenues," he said.

Business.title: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city
Business.text:
Every day $1bn worth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry.

News this week of Donald Trump’s escalating trade spat with Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”.

“We don’t need Canada, they need us,” Trump declared.

But many are hoping that Trump’s imposition of 50% tariffs on Canadian goods this week will not last long, with the upcoming midterm elections as a pivotal reason the plan may be scrapped.

Control of the US Congress hangs in the balance and will almost certainly be decided by several close Michigan races. It also comes just two months after polling highlighted Michiganders’ fatigue with and opposition to the president’s unprecedented tariff program.

By a 63%-31% margin, residents here oppose tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a June Epic-MRA poll, including 35% of Republicans. Meanwhile, nearly 75% of Michiganders said the tariffs are fueling high prices.

Trump doubling down on an unpopular policy deep into election season is viewed by many observers as a gift to Democrats, and there is a real possibility that it contributes to a midterm loss for the Republicans. Meanwhile, there seems to be little upside for Trump.

“I don’t understand what Trump is thinking,” the Epic-MRA pollster Bernie Porn said.

Regardless, Michiganders have already suffered disproportionately as they pay on average over $3,200 annually for tariffs, or about 142% more than the rest of the country, because of the state’s shared border with Canada.

The Canadian economy would also take a major hit if the tariffs are imposed, said Patrick Anderson, a Michigan-based economist with the Anderson Economic Group.

“Both will suffer – there are no two ways about it,” Anderson added.

This critical upper midwest swing state has picked the presidential winner in five consecutive elections, going from Barack Obama to Trump to Joe Biden and back to Trump. Democrats’ chances to retake the Senate rest heavily on the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed beating Trump ally Mike Rogers in the 3 November general election race. Rogers has supported the tariffs, but so far has been silent on the latest escalation.

The tariffs and the unpopular Iran war’s contribution to inflation represent a “double hit” for Republicans, Porn said, and Trump is handing ammo to a particularly adept candidate in El-Sayed. He has energized people with his anti-establishment, populist political vision, and a no-holds-barred delivery.

“El-Sayed has proven to be very, very articulate on a number of issues,” Porn added. “I think that he is going to try and just throw bombs at Rogers [in an upcoming debate] because Rogers supports these tariffs and trade war. Trump’s low popularity is an anchor around Rogers’ neck.”

In a statement, El-Sayed hammered Trump and Rogers, saying that the president “cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis.

“Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price,” El-Sayed said. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long, and Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber-stamp them.”

El-Sayed said he would push for “real, fair trade deals that create good-paying jobs”. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has 350,000 members in Michigan and is often a political kingmaker here, has supported some of Trump’s targeted tariffs, but said in a statement it “rejects” the latest escalation.

“If we’re going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions,” the UAW president, Shawn Fain, said. Canada has strong unions, and the UAW supports those.

“Tariffs work, but only if they are deployed intentionally to protect workers and grow our manufacturing communities, and it’s time to permanently end offshoring and the race to the bottom,” Fain added.

Mexico and Canada currently face 25% US tariffs on autos, though partial exemptions in the nations’ free trade agreement make the effective rate much lower, overall. Anderson estimated tariffs cost US auto companies about $12.5bn in 2025.

The Canadian government has announced it will impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of goods starting 8 September. The actions leading to the latest blow-up have been “rife with miscalculations, overreactions, and hubris”, Anderson said. He read through the list of goods on which tariffs would be imposed – feathers, sweaters, girls’ dresses, lobster.

“This is not a trade war. This is an annoyance list. Chest pounding,” Anderson said.

The North American auto industry over the last 60 years has integrated across the continent, and auto parts cross a border an average of six times before they land in a final product. That means there would be shared pain, Anderson said, and it would reverberate across the upper midwest, where bigger manufacturing cities are typically powered by industries that are often reliant on international trade.

But the Canadian economy is smaller, and Ontario’s economy is so concentrated that it would hit harder north of the border, Anderson added. Ultimately, the real threat is that “these two countries go pell-mell into it” and impose tariffs on oil, energy and commodities that hit harder than lobster.

The dialogue has devolved into the usual petty antagonism that is a hallmark of Trump’s beefs. Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, and Vice-President JD Vance referred to Canada as the 51st state.

“Let me say with great understatement that this is not helpful,” Anderson added.

Indeed, the Windsor mayor, Drew Dilkens, took exception to that particular comment. In an interview, he expressed deep frustration over Trump’s moves, and labeled justifications Trump has used for issuing tariffs, including framing them as a response to illegal immigration on the northern border, “nonsense”.

The latest escalation “is an aggressive move, one that could not be ignored by our country”, added Dilkens, who leads the city of 230,000 people. “It’s just offensive that he launches these attacks at Canada, who is your largest trading partner, your closest ally, and your neighbor.”

The chaos has cooled investment in Windsor, and prices remain high on both sides of the border. He pointed out how much more US consumers are paying not just for automobiles, but for beef, which in part stems from tariffs on Canadian beef.

“What is really crazy is that he is willing to throw his own citizens under the bus to pursue his tariff agenda,” Dilkens said. “They have Donald Trump to thank.”

Highlighting the tension among the president and some in his base, the Michigan chamber of commerce, a trade organization that lobbies on behalf of the state’s largest corporations, normally vocally supports the president on economic issues. It has not made a public statement, and did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.

However, the typically pro-Trump Detroit chamber of commerce did not mince words.

“Escalating tensions and tariffs will only cause economic pain on both sides of the border, especially in Michigan and the binational Detroit-Windsor region,” the chamber said in a press statement, adding that global competitors like China benefited most.

“Our economies are intertwined, interconnected, and stronger together; the sooner normalcy is restored the better.”

Business.title: Fed chair says delivering ‘stable prices’ is central bank’s job as inflation persists
Business.text:
The US Federal Reserve is not done fighting high inflation, its chair, Kevin Warsh, said in his first major speech in the role on Friday, emphasizing that it was “the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices”.

Warsh did not indicate where the Fed will take interest rates in the coming months, despite US inflation remaining stubbornly above the central bank’s 2% target amid the war in Iran. But his speech was taken by markets as a signal that rates may rise in the coming months, a move that may put him at odds with Donald Trump, who has aggressively called for rates to be cut.

The Fed chair painted a rosy view of the economy that contrasts with recent data. He said the economy “appears to have strengthened” given how it has held up to shocks.

“On that score, both Main Street and Wall Street have been resilient,” Warsh said at the Fed’s annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on Friday.

The Jackson Hole symposium has typically served as a platform for Fed chairs to offer clarity on the central bank’s general direction. For example, former Fed chair Jerome Powell foreshadowed rate cuts at his keynote address last year.

But Warsh on Friday insisted the days of such “forward guidance” were over, saying that the practice was adopted by the Fed during the 2008 financial crisis. “As with other legacies of crises past, I believe that the practice has overstayed its welcome,” he said.

Markets are still expected to carefully gauge Warsh’s speech for signs of the Fed’s next move. At the central bank’s last board meeting in July, three out of 12 voting members wanted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point – the first time in a decade so many board members shared dissent over a policy position. But a majority of the members voted to hold rates, which currently sit at a range of 3.5% to 3.75%, steady.

Since he was appointed in May, Warsh has had to strike a delicate balance between managing an economy that has been shaken by higher oil prices brought on by the war in Iran without provoking the ire of the White House. Trump has continued to insist the Fed should lower interest rates, despite economists who warn that that would further exacerbate inflation. After hitting a three-year high of 4.2% in May, US inflation cooled to 3.4% in July – still 1% higher than figures seen last year.

Warsh said progress on inflation over the past several years has been “modest”, and though price readings from over the summer came in better than expected, they did not indicate that “underlying trends have meaningfully improved”.

The US bond market has been particularly sensitive to higher inflation, with the yield on 10-year notes hitting its highest level since 2007 in recent weeks. Yields briefly went down after the US treasury announced a big debt buy-back scheme, though the relief proved to be temporary. Rising rates in the US have driven yields higher abroad – bond rates in the UK, Germany, France and Japan have all hit their highest levels in decades. Meanwhile, the US gross national debt topped $40tn for the first time in history last week.

In reaction to Warsh’s opening remarks, the two-year and 10-year US treasury yields increased slightly, while the 30-year treasury remained largely the same. The S&P 500 remained leveled while the Dow Jones ticked down slightly.

Business.title: Ex-Barclays boss denies having sex with woman dressed as Snow White after Epstein emails
Business.text:
The former Barclays boss Jes Staley has denied having sex with a woman dressed as Snow White, after being questioned about an infamous email exchange about Disney princesses with Jeffrey Epstein.

The comments were detailed in newly released transcripts from a closed-door interview last month with US lawmakers as part of their investigation into Epstein, who died in prison in August 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

In the email exchange on 9 and 10 July 2010 Staley and Epstein referred to Disney princesses. In those messages, the details of which have been circulating in the media since 2021, Staley tells Epstein: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.”

Epstein then asks: “What character would you like next?” to which Staley replied: “Beauty and the Beast.” Epstein responded: “Well one side is availble [sic].”

During his congressional testimony, Staley, who spent more than three decades at JPMorgan Chase before joining Barclays in 2015, was asked: “Did you ever have sex with a young woman in a Snow White costume?

“No, I did not,” Staley said.

Lawmakers then questioned Staley about another email, sent to Epstein by an unnamed individual on 10 July 2010 and which said: “the snow white was f..ed twice as soon as she put her costume))”. Epstein appears to have asked an unnamed individual to buy a Snow White costume weeks before those exchanges, on 20 June 2010.

“Why would this young woman have sent this email to Mr. Epstein if the two of you had not had sex while she was wearing a Snow White costume and if Mr. Epstein had not instructed her to do so?” a congressional representative, whose name has been redacted from the transcript, asked.

“I have no idea who else she was with. I – it has nothing to do with me, though,” Staley said. When pressed further, he said: “I may have seen her in apartment [sic] and prompted that email. But I was not with a person dressed as Snow White outside of potentially crossing at his apartment.”

The representative asked: “So you may have seen her in his apartment, later emailed Mr. Epstein and said, ‘That was fun,’ but it was not because you had sex with her?”

“That’s correct,” Staley said.

In the transcript, Staley is then asked: “Would you agree that’s a pretty incredible coincidence, that you email him on July 9th, saying, ‘That was fun, say hi to Snow White,’ and then [the unnamed individual] emails him the next day, reporting back on something that just didn’t have anything to do with you?”

“Sure. Why not?” Staley said.

“That’s pretty hard to believe,” the representative said.

The former banker was also asked whether he and Epstein used “Disney princesses as code names for selecting women for sexual encounters”, to which Staley replied, “No.”

Staley’s reputation has been tarnished as a result of his well-documented friendship with the child sex offender.

Staley originally met Epstein in 2000 after he became head of JP Morgan’s private bank, where Epstein was a client. Staley later took over as chief executive of Barclays, one of the UK’s largest banks, in 2015 but was forced to step down in 2021 after City regulators opened an investigation into his relationship with Epstein.

Business.title: CEOs earn 614 times more than workers at US’s 100 lowest-paying corporations
Business.text:
The average CEO of the US’s 100 largest, lowest-paying corporations earned 614 times more than their average worker last year, according to an analysis by the Institute for Policy Studies (IPS).

IPS’s latest executive excess report analyzed compensation at the 100 S&P 500 corporations with the lowest median worker pay. Between 2019 and 2025, CEO compensation increased 41.4%, unadjusted for inflation, twice as much as the median worker pay increased at these firms during the same period, at 20.7%.

Inflation also outpaced worker pay increases, rising by 25.9%.

The CEO-to-worker pay ratio at the low-wage 100 firms increased 8.4% between 2019 and 2025.

The average CEO compensation among low-wage 100 corporations was $17.5m in 2025, compared with median worker pay of $36,571.

The wealth of at least 36 billionaires is linked to these low-wage 100 corporations, including Walmart’s eight Walton family members, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos and Mackenzie Scott, and Carvana co-founders Ernie Garcia II and Ernie Garcia III.

“This is really a big problem for society, that we have such extremes,” said Sarah Anderson, lead author of the report and director of the Global Economy Project at the Institute for Policy Studies.

“To me, it seems like these CEOs are just living on a remote economic planet from the one that their employees are living on, and it makes it really hard for them to fathom what it’s like to have to worry about putting food on your family’s table or even coming home at night if you are at risk of being detained by ICE.”

The report notes that the low-wage 100 corporations have a combined force of 1,282 registered federal lobbyists and that many of these companies did not denounce aggressive immigration enforcement actions toward their workforce or on their property.

“Low-wage workers are now facing the biggest cuts to Medicaid and Snap [food benefits] in history. Many of the employees at these companies have to rely on those programs, and then so many of them have also been terrorized and detained by ICE agents,” added Anderson. “So it’s really astounding that the leaders of these companies have turned a blind eye to this surge of threats against many of their workers, and instead they’ve just continue to be fixated on enriching themselves.”

Stock buybacks among these firms increased in 2025, to $108.6bn from $105bn in 2024. Between 2019 and 2025, the low-wage 100 firms spent $718bn on stock buybacks.

Among the 100 low-wage firms, Walmart spent the most on stock buybacks, at $8.1bn, equivalent to a $3,851 bonus to each of the company’s 2.1 million workers. Walmart’s CEO, Doug McMillan, who stepped down in January 2026, received $29.2m in compensation in 2025, 958 times more than the median worker pay at Walmart of $30,520.

The report cites several policy solutions to excessive executive pay at corporations, including a tax hike on corporations that pay CEOs more than 50 times what they pay their median employees, an increase on stock buyback taxes and leveraging government contracts and subsidies to bar contractors from engaging in stock buybacks.

Walmart did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Sports.title: Sports Direct's Ashley attacks Burnham over 'populist' High Street revival plans
Sports.text:
Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has criticised Prime Minister Andy Burnham's cost of living and retail policies as "populist".

In a letter to Burnham, Ashley accused him of "jumping on 'everyday fixes' or bandwagons" while businesses struggled with the government's "disastrous" business rates policies and higher employment costs.

He also described a proposal to increase business rates on large warehouses in order to help reduce rates for pubs and clubs as "delusional".

A Downing Street spokesperson said Burnham would "build a new economy that backs British business, delivers growth in every postcode and ensures the essentials in life... are affordable again"

Removing the VAT from household electricity bills and reducing business rates for some firms was "just the start", the government spokesperson added.

Burnham has promised to revitalise Britain's "hollowed out" High Streets and to address cost of living concerns by tackling "rip-off Britain" including misleading discounting in shops.

Ashley's Frasers Group was built on buying up struggling brands and undercutting rivals on price. It is still owned by Ashley but now run by his son-in-law Michael Murray.

The business currently owns Sports Direct, Flannels, House of Fraser, Game, Evans Cycles, Slazenger, Jack Wills, and Gieves & Hawkes, and several other retail brands.

Ashley's letter, seen by the BBC and first reported by the Financial Times,, external hits out at the government's strategy.

"Shortsighted or populist reactions to underlying business challenges are not the answer. You have the chance to make a difference or get it horribly wrong," he wrote.

He called on Burnham to use his first Budget, scheduled for 28 October, to lower costs for employers and address business rates.

The government has launched a review of the tax on commercial properties, but in advance of that has already announced that pubs, social clubs and live music venues will get a 20% business rates cut from April.

"If your answer is to tax larger retailers even more, through hiking business rates on retailer-owned or third-party warehouses whilst reducing rates for pubs and clubs, then that is simply delusional," Ashley's letter said.

Burnham previously said before he was prime minister that cuts for pubs, clubs and music venues could be paid for by higher levies on warehouses operated by online firms such as Amazon, and targeting the owners of empty High Street properties.

Ashley built Frasers Group from a single Sports Direct store in Maidenhead in 1982 to a sprawling empire of dozens of brands employing 30,000 people.

The billionaire has frequently attracted controversy from investors and the media with accusations over the years of building success by exploiting workers.

In 2016, Ashley admitted to MPs that workers at his Derbyshire warehouse had been paid below the minimum wage and a policy of fining staff for being late was unacceptable.

The business this month bought luxury department store Harvey Nichols and promised a "significant restructuring" of the business.

In his letter to Burnham he asks: "My challenge to you is – how are you going to help with turning Harvey Nichols around?"

He also raises the issue of retail theft which he said cost Frasers Group approximately £40m a year.

Frasers Group has also been increasing its stake in menswear retailer Hugo Boss after its initial takeover bid for the German company was rejected.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace 1-4 Man City: Rayan Cherki impresses in big away win
Sports.text:
Rayan Cherki refuses to hide his emotions, an open book for all to see and hear in times of joy and disappointment.

Moments after Manchester City had put down their first heavyweight marker of the post-Pep Guardiola era by brushing aside Crystal Palace, he was asked live on TV how much he enjoyed the game. Rather than providing the usual textbook answer, he instead gave a colourfully uncomplimentary – and unprintable - description of his own first-half performance.

Erling Haaland, standing alongside Cherki as he waited to hand over the player-of-the-match award, could only laugh at the France attacker's sweary honesty.

Indeed, the 23-year-old also refuses to hide his talent, making a nonsense of his self-criticism by unveiling a Selhurst Park masterclass with two brilliant second-half goals in the 4-1 victory.

Cherki made his impact under Guardiola last season, although there was always a feeling the mercurial signing from Lyon for a bargain £30m could produce more. He made 33 Premier League appearances - but 14 of those were as a substitute.

And there is a sense that he already has something to prove under new boss Enzo Maresca amid City's vast attacking resources, coming off the bench to assist the two late goals that gave them victory against Bournemouth on the opening weekend.

Cherki was seen in animated conversation with Maresca after the final whistle, but his reward was a start at Selhurst Park and he delivered the sort of irresistible performance he, as well as City, needed.

He had a disappointing World Cup with France, reduced to a bit-part player, only starting against England in the third-fourth place play-off, being replaced at half-time with his side 4-0 down.

There were also videos that emerged with Cherki showing apparent displeasure at coach Didier Deschamps.

Cherki has a reputation for unpredictability, with Maresca saying after his contribution against Bournemouth that "if he is not happy he wants to show it".

But, though he has proved hard to please in the past at Leicester City and Chelsea, Maresca was satisfied with Cherki here.

"He's happy and I'm happy," said Maresca. "It was not just his performance with the two goals, but his work off the ball.

"He pressed and gave us a complete performance on the ball and off the ball.

"Rayan is Rayan. We know him. He loves football and it makes it so much easier to work with him.

"The quality he has in this moment helps the team, not just with assists but goals."

It was not just Cherki's wizardry with the ball that impressed Maresca, but his work off it.

"His performance off the ball was unbelievable," he added to BBC Match of the Day. "Everyone knows his quality but when he works hard off the ball, he was in charge of Adam Wharton. He controlled him. He was very good."

Praise indeed as the outstanding Wharton is one of the players City have cast their eyes over as they try to strengthen Maresca's squad before the close of the transfer window.

For all the team work that brought such praise from Maresca, it was the two moments of individual genius that will be remembered after a win and performance that suggested talk that City will inevitably go into decline after the departure of Guardiola has been greatly exaggerated.

He also produced those defining moments at crucial times, the first coming nine minutes into the second half with City leading 1-0 and Palace hoping to mount a recovery.

Cherki took Phil Foden's pass on the edge of the area, embarking on a slalom run surrounded by four Palace defenders, leaving them helpless before poking a left-foot finish past keeper Dean Henderson.

He celebrated with a touch of arrogance that is so often the preserve of the special ones, staring down the Palace fans on the Holmesdale Road end.

And after Palace pulled one back, it was Cherki who once again restored that two-goal advantage with a rising right-foot shot from 20 yards past Henderson.

Former England midfielder Jamie Redknapp told Sky Sports: "After Rayan Cherki painted a masterpiece, City started to play and got a real hold of it.

"Cherki felt like the difference because his goals came at an important time. He is a genius. The things he can do with a football are absolute genius.

"There aren't many Premier League players I've seen that can do this on the first goal.

"Eden Hazard possibly, he was that kind of player. Georgi Kinkladze, there'll be Manchester City fans from a previous generation who'll remember him, who could get past people in a telephone box. This was very similar.

"Once Cherki is in the box, they are so scared to touch him. It's absolute genius. He's an absolute bargain at £30m and gives you a new dimension. He gives you that 'X-factor'. He does things differently.

Cherki's goal celebrations summed up his confidence and attitude, with Redknapp saying: "There was a bit of Cantona about him. He's a beautiful player. With someone like Cherki you've got to let him do his thing."

There may be ups and downs between the maverick Cherki and the demanding Maresca, but the France star with stardust in his boots showed he will not be pushed to the back of the queue among City's array of attacking talent – with perhaps more to come before the deadline.

And that is good news for Maresca as he tried to build on the foundations left behind by Guardiola.

Sports.title: England vs Pakistan: Archer, Robinson, Tongue and Atkinson impress and 'could trouble Australia'
Sports.text:
Exciting or too early to say?

Any praise for England's pace attack this summer comes with the caveat of the quality of Pakistan's batting - and the fact they are operating in helpful home conditions.

But, after having their hand forced by the retirement of Ben Stokes, England have stumbled on something encouraging.

A four-man pace attack of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson, who dismissed Pakistan for 110 on day two of the second Test at Lord's, appears potent and, perhaps crucially for the future, are complementing each other in different ways...

After the first-Test win at Headingley, captain Joe Root said his pace bowlers "do not know how good they can be" and praised the variety they offer.

Root suggested this group is ahead of bowling stocks from his previous stint as captain, when he often called upon right-arm seamers James Anderson, Stuart Broad, Chris Woakes and Ben Stokes, in terms of their variation.

The most obvious differential between his new quartet is pace - something brought into further focus by England's decision to prioritise bowlers who reach high speeds during last winter's Ashes defeat.

While Archer was touching 95mph in the quickest opening spell of his career on day two at Lord's, Robinson was operating around 78mph at the other end.

Tongue's average pace across the series is actually higher than Archer, though Archer has bowled a higher percentage of his deliveries over 90mph.

Atkinson slots in just below Tongue and Archer, who joked he could play until he is 40 given how his team-mates are sharing the load.

"It is a good attack," said former England captain Michael Vaughan. "They can all get better and that is a really good sign.

"This batting line-up is possibly the easiest I have seen to bowl to but this attack, bowling the way they are doing, will challenge better batting line-ups.

"They will challenge the Australia line-up quite nicely if they bowl like this."

What Robinson has lacked in pace, he is making up for with skill. Four more wickets on Friday took him to 17 wickets at an average of 8.84 across his three Tests this summer.

Helped by lively English pitches, Robinson has been able to concentrate on his greatest skill - his control of line and length.

Against Pakistan, he has hit a good length with 70% of his deliveries. Atkinson has the next best record with 52%.

It has meant Robinson has been relentlessly testing the defences of Pakistan's batters, while giving them few bad balls to hit.

He bowled 31 deliveries in a row without conceding a run on Friday and 13 overs, which cost only 11 runs, were the most economical figures by a pace bowler bowling 10 overs or more in England for 13 years.

"Ollie Robinson is an extraordinarily skillful bowler," said Vaughan.

"[England] are trying to get him to 81mph more consistently and if he can get to that he will challenge all batting line-ups in all conditions.

"He has been the tone-setter we were crying out for in the winter."

Archer's natural angle makes him particularly effective against left-handers.

He averages 23.9 against southpaws compared with 31.3 against right-handers - helpful for England because Tongue and Atkinson's records are almost a mirror image.

Tongue averages 21.5 against right-handers but 35.7 against lefties. Atkinson's record is 19.9 compared with 31.7.

Tongue's position on the crease also aids him in his speciality of targeting the stumps.

Across this series, 22% of Tongue's deliveries would have hit the timbers while a figure of 29% at Headingley, where he took eight wickets across the first Test, was the highest by an England bowler in a home Test for 15 years.

And after two more wickets on Friday, Tongue's bowling strike-rate now stands at a dismissal once every 39.8 balls, putting him 12th on the list of bowlers to have taken 30 Test wickets.

"Tongue is the one who is really developing the best of them," Agnew said.

A home Ashes series is less than one year away. England's bowlers appear to be shaping up nicely.

Sports.title: Leon Baptiste: Other British athletes convicted in connection with coach's sex assault of minor in Morocco
Sports.text:
Three British former athletes were convicted in Morocco as part of an investigation into the sexual assault of a minor by a sprinting coach, BBC Sport can reveal.

The prosecutions led to the imprisonment of Leon Baptiste, a UK Athletics coach and 2010 Commonwealth Games gold medallist for England in the 200m.

Baptiste was originally reported as missing in Morocco in some media articles published on 14 August, before a BBC Sport investigation revealed his conviction and jailing.

Now, court rulings seen by BBC Sport shed more light on other convictions relating to the same case.

Two-time Commonwealth silver medallist hurdler Will Sharman, his brother and ex-bobsleigh athlete Richard Sharman, and fellow former bobsleigh competitor Lamin Deen, who were all on holiday with Baptiste, were convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.

Also convicted of the same offence were acquaintances Ashley O'Leary Jones and David Tuck.

The group said via their lawyers that they were never arrested and were unaware of their convictions until informed of them by BBC Sport.

A spokesperson for all five men told BBC Sport: "William, Richard, Lamin, David and Ashley are shocked and distressed by the circumstances in which they have unexpectedly found themselves.

"They reject any suggestion that they knowingly engaged in unlawful or improper conduct. They left Morocco believing they had complied with all requirements placed upon them.

"At the time, they understood that they had paid an administrative fine equivalent to approximately £40 and that the matter had concluded."

BBC Sport understands that police raided a villa in Tamensourt on the outskirts of Marrakech after a girl contacted them claiming she had been brought to the property, had not been paid money she was promised in exchange for sex with Baptiste, and that she had been assaulted by a housekeeper after she was accused of stealing a watch.

Baptiste, 41, was subsequently convicted of sexual assault of a minor and given a 10-month prison sentence, which was subsequently reduced to eight months on appeal.

Court documents refer to the girl as being 16 years old and say she suffered "psychological trauma, sexual exploitation, physical assault and injury, and the violation of her human dignity".

Court records show that in June the five men were given suspended sentences of four months and fines of 500 dirhams (£40) each after being convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.

All five men were acquitted of a separate charge of inciting a minor to engage in prostitution.

The Morocco presidency of the public ministry, which oversees prosecutions in the country, provided BBC Sport with the court judgement regarding the group, which reads: "The defendants were in the company of [Leon Baptiste] and were seated at the same table as the minor, alongside her.

"They thereby assisted him in deceiving the minor and persuading her to engage in sexual relations [with Baptiste]. This constitutes participation in the enticement of a minor.

"The court found them guilty on this count and decided to convict them for these acts."

The group had already left Morocco by the time the decision was handed down. Their convictions and sentences were upheld after an appeal hearing in July.

In a response provided by their lawyers to BBC Sport, the Sharman brothers, Deen, O’Leary Jones and Tuck say they visited the Montecristo nightclub based on a recommendation provided by their driver, and had no reason to believe it was anything other than a respectable establishment.

They say they were unaware of the girl's age and that some members of the group do not even recall seeing her in the nightclub. The villa they were staying in was vast and the interaction between the men and Mr Baptiste while inside the villa was limited.

They also say that they were not present in court on any occasion, that the court process was not in English and that it was not explained to them.

The spokesperson continued: "What has unfolded over recent months has been a distressing and incoherent saga.

"They did not properly understand the proceedings and were completely shocked on being told that they were the subject of a criminal conviction, when that is not how they understood it."

Companies House records and a biography on one of O'Leary Jones' social media profiles show he is a director of a company operating five children's care homes in Greater Manchester.

Tuck's social media biography indicates he is a military veteran, while a CV posted online lists experience coaching women's and children's football clubs including at Stoke City, Apollon Limassol in Cyprus, and Orlando Pride in the USA.

When asked by BBC Sport to comment on the convictions and the potential safeguarding issues raised, the UK Foreign Office, Home Office, and Department for Culture, Media, and Sport declined to provide a response.

Records also show that other people were convicted in relation to the case.

They include the housekeeper of the villa and two of its security guards, who were each given a two-month suspended prison sentence and a fine of 5,000 dirhams (£396).

The manager of the Montecristo nightclub where the group met the girl was sentenced to two months in jail.

A waiter at the Montecristo was also prosecuted, as was the owner of the agency which rents out the villa.

The girl - a Moroccan national - was awarded civil compensation of 60,000 dirhams (£4,784), to be paid jointly by all of those convicted, plus court costs.

Sports.title: Frank Lampard: Coventry boss on his managerial inspirations and proving doubters wrong
Sports.text:
The Football Interview will be available on BBC One at 12:45 every Saturday during the Premier League season, as well as on BBC iPlayer, BBC Football YouTube and the BBC Sport website and app.

In the second episode of the new season, available on Saturday, 29 August, musician Tom Grennan sits down with Coventry City manager Frank Lampard.

As a player, Frank Lampard worked under some of the biggest managers in the game, including Jose Mourinho, Carlo Ancelotti, Guus Hiddink and Rafael Benitez - not to mention his uncle Harry Redknapp.

Eight years into his own managerial career, the Coventry City boss cited Mourinho and Ancelotti as the main influences on his style.

"Jose and Carlo are like both sides of the coin," the 48-year-old told BBC Sport.

"Jose was very on you, he transmitted his self-confidence, but if you stepped out of line or did something wrong, you'd feel the strength of him, whereas Carlo was chilled and calm. When you look back, you go, 'that's a nice environment to work in'. It felt like he trusted you. So I try and take little snippets. I'm probably somewhere in the middle."

Lampard played under Mourinho and Ancelotti at Chelsea and won the Premier League and FA Cup with them both.

He said it is important to strike a balance between the pair as he targets more success with Coventry.

"I start to sometimes go towards being Jose, sometimes I go and be a bit more Carlo," he added.

"I've learnt that young managers, you come in and feel like you have to to criticise a bad performance or say something about an individual that turns up late. The more I've done this job, I realise that they're all humans.

"Sometimes a lad comes in late, you don't know the back story. And so trying to jump on him and being this hard man manager, you've got to be more Carlo. But then if you're a bit more relaxed sometimes and people are on the pitch, not doing their job, sometimes you've got a bit more Jose."

Lampard said he is not driven by trying to convince the sceptics after leading Coventry back to the Premier League for the first time in 25 years.

"The thing about modern-day football – you're brilliant one minute, you might not be brilliant the next and then everyone will let you know that," he told musician and Sky Blues fan Tom Grennan.

"You've got to be careful trying to prove every doubter wrong, because it's not possible."

Lampard guided Coventry to win the Championship with 95 points last season after taking over at the club in November 2024.

Prior to that, his managerial experience could be described as a mixed bag. After taking over at Derby in 2018, the former Chelsea midfielder led them to the Championship play-off final, where they lost to Aston Villa.

Following that, he had abortive spells in the Premier League with Chelsea and Everton, lasting 18 months at Stamford Bridge before being sacked in January 2021, and lasting less than a year at Goodison Park before being sacked in January 2023.

"My personal ambition to prove any doubters wrong is sort of always there, but I try not to let that be my driver," Lampard explained.

"I've been in the Premier League as a player, I've been as a manager, I understand the challenge of it. I can't get ahead of myself and I can't worry too much about the outside world because otherwise you succumb to it, you'd be making different decisions."

As a player, Lampard won three Premier League titles and the Champions League in 2012. He also won four FA Cups, two League Cups and the Europa League.

He described last season's promotion with Coventry as being on par with some of those achievements.

"When you get promoted, it's hard to balance against winning the Champions League with Chelsea," Lampard said.

"Winning in Munich was the best footballing night of my life as a player by far. But then when you do something with a club that's been through what it's been through, when you work with a group of lads that are so great as a dressing room - I've never experienced, especially as a coach, to have such a good group.

"When we got promoted against Blackburn, I had a rush of pure emotion, it all came on top of me. It certainly goes right up there in things I've managed to achieve."

Lampard said that his side will have to adapt to the different challenge this season after entering the top flight, especially defensively.

"We want to keep hold of the good things from last year," he added.

"We'd be fools to think that we'd just go and play like we did in the 'Champ' every week when we dominated a lot of games."

In terms of ambitions for the season, he wants his players to be brave.

"Everyone's going to ask me, 'staying in the league, is that your target?'," Lampard said.

"Of course it would be success, because it's such a big challenge for us, but in the beginning, we'll go into it and go, 'let's stick our chests out and let's be brave about it'.

"These boys have earned where they've got to, so go in with that attitude. There's a lot to lose, but go and show yourselves."

Coventry lost 3-0 to champions Arsenal in the opening match of the season. They will host fellow promoted side Hull City on Saturday, in their first home game of the campaign.

Sports.title: Imran Khan: Sarfaraz Ahmed says Pakistan players did not know about boycott threat
Sports.text:
Head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed said he and his players did not know about a Pakistan Cricket Board threat to the England and Wales Cricket Board over a Sky interview with the sons of Imran Khan.

During lunch on day one of the second Test, Sky Sports aired an interview with Suleiman and Kasim Khan, the sons of former Pakistan captain and prime minister Imran, who has been in prison for the past three years.

It is understood the PCB raised the prospect of cancelling the Test at Lord's and the remainder of the three-match tour if the interview aired.

A version of the interview was broadcast, and the players returned to the field after the interval to continue the match.

"I don't know anything. I'm just focusing on the match," said Sarfaraz at the end of the second day's play.

"You're talking about the interview? We don't know about the interview."

Asked if there was ever a possibility his players would return for the afternoon session on day one, the former Pakistan wicketkeeper said: "All are OK. We were having lunch at that time."

Legendary all-rounder Imran Khan, 73, had a 21-year international career for Pakistan and famously led his team to World Cup glory in 1992.

He served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022. Since 2023, Khan has been in jail on corruption charges which he denies.

The PCB chairman Mohsin Naqvi also serves as Pakistan's interior minister.

In the interview conducted by former England captain Michael Atherton, Suleiman and Kasim expressed concerns over the treatment and security given to their father, as well as criticising the UK government's response.

Before it aired, Sky received a complaint about the plan to broadcast the interview.

In response to the tension around the situation, the ECB took government advice from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.

In Pakistan, the match is being aired by the public broadcaster PTV, using Sky's pictures. PTV did not air the interview.

Ultimately, the tourists resumed play after lunch and the Test has continued to the end of the second day, with England 261 runs ahead at 81-3 in their second innings.

It is understood Sky received no further complaints on Friday in relation to the interview.

In October, England will tour Pakistan for a one-day tri-series against the home side and Sri Lanka.

It will be England's fourth separate tour of Pakistan in the past four years following a 17-year gap between visits to the country because of security concerns.

In 2006, a Test between England and Pakistan at The Oval was abandoned after the visitors were accused of ball tampering.

Pakistan were adjudged to have forfeited the match after refusing to play after tea on the fourth day, the only instance in Test history when a team has forfeited a Test.

Sports.title: US Open 2026: Katie Boulter won't repeat Andy Murray wedding ring mistake as she prepares for final major of season
Sports.text:
Andy Murray has long been a guiding figure for British tennis, but newly-married Katie Boulter will not be following his lead when it comes to keeping her wedding ring safe.

Three-time Grand Slam champion Murray, who married wife Kim in 2015, famously briefly lost his wedding band after playing with it tied to his shoe laces.

Murray had left his trainers - with the ring still attached - under a car to dry out after a practice session in California in 2021, and after discovering they were missing the next day, was eventually reunited with both after putting out an appeal for their return.

Boulter, who married Australia's world number seven Alex de Minaur this summer, said she will not be making the same mistake.

"I learned from Andy. I'm not going to do that," the 30-year-old said. "I don't wear it. Not during matches."

Boulter and De Minaur tied the knot at a small, private ceremony in England before holding a bigger celebration in Tuscany, Italy, in July.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Boulter said: "One was in the UK for my nearest and dearest. It was like eight people - very, very small, very much for my grandpa.

"It was a huge contrast to the Italian wedding, which had all of our closest people, all of our friends, and was a little bit more of a party and a lot of fun."

When it came to De Minaur's speech, however, Boulter admitted she was "sceptical".

"I hadn't seen him do any preparation for the speech at all. And he was like, 'I'm just going to wing it. It's fine. How hard can it be?'," she said.

"He was amazing. He was so, good. I was crying the whole time. I think I permanently cried for like three hours straight during all the speeches."

Since their wedding, the world number 60 has wasted no time in throwing herself back into tennis before the US Open, which gets under way on Sunday.

"I actually just chose to go straight back into the conditions, go into the deep end and see what we've got," said Boulter, who lost in the first round in Washington and Toronto before suffering a second-round exit in Cincinnati.

"I do think the conditions in the States are very different from the UK. I think you can't really replicate them.

"So I felt like I'd be a little underprepared coming to the US and just getting used to the conditions again would have been quite difficult."

Boulter's US Open begins with a first-round encounter against American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee, who is ranked 143rd in the world.

A record four British players have made it through qualifying to reach the main draw at the US Open.

Fran Jones, Harriet Dart and Harry Wendelken all won their third and final qualifying matches on Friday, while Toby Samuel advanced on Thursday after his opponent, Chile's Cristian Garin, retired during a lengthy rain delay.

It is the first time that four British players have progressed from qualifying at an overseas Grand Slam since the Australian Open of 1988.

Jacob Fearnley lost to Austria's Jurij Rodionov in a rain-disrupted match that stretched across Thursday and Friday, but the 25-year-old will play Spain's Martin Landaluce in the first round after securing a main draw spot as a lucky loser.

The five Britons will join compatriots Arthur Fery, Cameron Norrie, Jan Choinski and Boulter in the main draws.

Wendelken earned his first appearance in the main draw at an overseas Grand Slam as he fought back to beat Lithuania's Vilius Gaubas 6-7 (3-7) 7-6 (7-5) 7-6 (10-5).

He will face Italian 22nd seed Luciano Darderi in the first round, while Samuel is up against the Czech Republic's Tomas Machac.

Jones, meanwhile, claimed a straightforward 6-4 6-1 win over Taiwan's Joanna Garland to qualify for a second successive year and set up a first-round meeting with Poland's Magda Linette

Meanwhile, Heather Watson missed out on her first US Open singles main-draw appearance in five years as Dart fought back from a set and a break down to win 2-6 6-4 6-1.

"It's never easy playing against a friend and Heather is such an a great player and has so much experience," Dart told BBC Sport.

"It showed for an hour and a half, I was really behind and she was playing some really good tennis. In the end I was able to stick to it somehow and find a way and turn it in my favour."

Dart, who has reached the second round in her last two main draw appearances at Flushing Meadows, will play American Peyton Stearns in the first round.

Sports.title: Craig Kirby: How one 50-year-old footballer became a viral inspiration
Sports.text:
Above a Methodist church at the end of a row of terraced housing, north of Rochdale town centre, Craig Kirby's phone is buzzing as he opens the door to his gym. The 50-year-old's latest TikTok video has just crept over 85,000 views.

It shows a personal highlights reel from one of his amateur football matches, filmed from the touchline by wife Lindsay, with a caption explaining how Kirby finds space and time on the bobbly park pitch. "Fitness and movement off the ball are 90% of the game," the text adds.

Kirby smiles at the video going viral. It has racked up more than 340,000 views by the time of writing, but it is nothing new.

The one pinned to the top of his profile has been seen 2.9 million times. It's a compilation of him playing for Whitworth Valley against Old Rivingtonians on a drizzly January afternoon, a backdrop of rolling Lancashire hills and a kids' playground, a simple title of: "Well beaten today. Not bad for 50 though."

That is one of his earliest videos from the beginning of last season - since then he has continued to post regularly across TikTok and Instagram, where the midfielder's 'Football at 50' profile has about 30,000 followers on each.

Kirby, dealing with unimaginable grief following the death of son Sebastian in December 2023, had considered quitting football.

But his wife encouraged him to play on, suggesting she would film his matches. They thought a handful of family and close friends might watch them.

"I put it on and it went to over one million views," explains Kirby. "We were like: 'Wow?!' Lots of things have happened since and it has made me reevaluate.

"I am probably enjoying football right now more than I did in my late 20s or early 30s."

Kirby is undoubtedly a talented player. He had trials at Blackburn Rovers as a teenager but was already set on following his dad into the army. When he left in his mid 20s, there were opportunities at Cambridge United and Kettering but none that would support his young family.

His hair is whiter now, distinguishing him from younger opponents, but as a personal trainer the physique is still there - Kirby even says he is doing sprint training to work on becoming quicker this season.

Most videos show clips from his games, but Kirby also documents himself training, juggling a ball in his gym or doing keepy-ups against a wall.

He avoids posting any of the aggro that can be found in amateur football to instead focus on neat touches and clever passes, the analysis of an odd error. The response has been overwhelmingly positive.

For every 'Sergio Bus Pass' comment there are hundreds praising his technique, comparing him to Zinedine Zidane or explaining what an inspiration he is.

"We're always worried about red flags and being sold this scary world," says Kirby.

"But most people are just trying to get on and looking for someone to look up to or to inspire them to do something.

"I hope I can do that for some people my age who think 'I'm too old'."

Kirby has been both surprised and delighted by the opportunities that have come with his newfound exposure.

He is playing for Vauxhall Motors in the Cheshire Veterans League Premier Division this season, where they will come up against Wythenshawe's all-star cast of former professionals.

Kirby has already struck up a friendship with ex-Newcastle striker Papiss Cisse, who praised his left foot. Eight-time Olympic champion Usain Bolt is the latest star to register with Wythenshawe - and Kirby jokes those extra hill sprints might come in handy.

He is a regular at games hosted by other content creators now too, some draw hundreds of spectators and Kirby is touched when young fans recognise him and ask for his shirt.

In fact, while he places an emphasis on trying to encourage people to continue sport into their latter years - both for social and physical benefits - Kirby is keen to stress youngsters should not lose the love for football either.

"Everyone should just be enjoying putting their boots on and if they become a professional, wow, that's amazing," he says.

"But I just think there's a lot of pressure from a very young age to get into an academy or some sort of pathway.

"And I just think you're missing out on what I had - on the common with my friends, crushing a can and kicking it because we didn't have a football. I'm not saying it's all wrong, but we have to consider just having fun, which I have done for 40 years."

One of Kirby's proudest moments, though, has been his call-up for England's over-50s team - he's played in several friendlies and hopes to win his first official cap in Thailand later this year.

"I do love my country and it's a real privilege to wear the kit and you do feel like you're an England player," says Kirby. "Some of the guys have played at such a good level, some ex-pros, some non-league guys."

But there is a deeper fuel underpinning Kirby's motivation to keep playing. Almost three years ago, his 20-year-old son died by suicide while serving in the Royal Air Force in Norway. It followed the death of one of Sebastian's friends months earlier.

"He was such a positive kid," says Kirby. "I was going to retire because of it, and I thought I can't quit the game I love on grief. And 99% of the time I am good, but it is always there, and when I go on the pitch, it's about Seb."

Kirby's wife Lindsay praises his positive attitude for helping the family during the most difficult times, and he has spoken candidly about mental health and grief in his videos. If you are feeling vulnerable, he says, it can help to talk.

"I have had people tell me they have lost everything because of grief and they are rethinking what they've done," adds Kirby.

"Because they have made bad habits when the grief happened, they have leaned on them - drugs, alcohol, gambling, they've ended up losing their house and their family, and that is one of the things I wanted to not happen.

"Because I have always had positive outlets for my energy, I think I have leaned on that a bit more and rather than spiralling, I was able to create a direction to go in."

Football - and sharing what was supposed to be one last season - has helped Kirby, but is also now helping others too.

His advice to those also wanting to pull their boots back on is simple.

"Things are easy if you just do them," he says. "The actual friction and the hard work comes from thinking about doing them. If you want to go for a run and you can't be bothered, do it anyway. That's how I've been and how I still am."

Indeed, when we first talk, Kirby is on his way to watch England Over-75s play Germany on the anniversary of the 1966 World Cup final. So how long will he go on?

"As soon as someone goes past me and they're laughing, I will probably stop then!"

Sports.title: Super League: St Helens 6-34 Leeds Rhinos - Rhinos go back top
Sports.text:
Betfred Super League

Tries: Welsby Goals: Sailor

Tries: Hankinson, Smith, Newman, Hall, Handley, Croft Goals: Connor 5

Leeds Rhinos moved back to the top of Super League on points difference with a rare and comprehensive away win at St Helens.

The Rhinos' first win at Saints since March 2023 means they will secure their first League Leaders' Shield for 11 years if they beat second-placed Wigan in a decider for the trophy next Saturday.

Cameron Smith scored the pick of the Rhinos' six tries on the night with a stunning individual effort as they raced into a commanding 18-point lead at the break.

Defeat for St Helens signals a damaging blow to their hopes of making this season's play-offs, failing to capitalise on Hull KR's heavy defeat last night by Wigan, staying two points below the sixth-placed Robins with two games remaining.

After an impeccably observed minute's silence in honour of the late Sir Billy Boston by everyone inside the Brewdog Stadium, an incisive dash and short ball from Jake Connor allowed Chris Hankinson to crash over from close range to break the deadlock.

Leeds momentarily thought they had scored a second try in two minutes as Cooper Jenkins went over under the sticks but Brodie Croft was penalised for a forward pass when attempting to knock the ball backwards.

While down to 12 men because of Daniel Suluka-Fifita's hit on Presley Cassell off the ball, Saints thought they were over but Tristan Sailor's lofted pass to Deon Cross was spotted to be forward as the winger dived in at the left corner.

Second-rower Smith then broke a tackle from Suluka-Fifita, back on the field, and gave the Saints backline a clean set of heels before getting down low to finish off an outstanding individual score.

The match was effectively taken away from Saints when slick hands from Connor set up Ash Handley who in turn found Harry Newman to dive over unopposed as Connor slotted the extras to give Leeds an 18-point lead at the break.

Tom Holroyd had a try disallowed a minute after half-time, unable to ground the ball before knocking on under pressure from Saints full-back Sailor.

Leeds did get their fourth try soon after though when Jack Bird's beautiful backhanded offload freed up Ryan Hall to dot down his 357th career try.

Saints were on the board when Jack Welsby's line break saw him race clear of Leeds' midfield and full-back Lachie Miller for the match's second excellent individual try.

But that proved to be just brief respite as Handley got on the scoresheet, latching on to a grubber kick from Connor, and another grubber from Connor found his half-back partner Croft, via the upright, for his 28th Super League try of the season.

Connor missed a penalty late on, striking the post, but his kicking game continues to impress with Leeds looking strong going into the upcoming play-offs.

Saints, meanwhile, will have to beat Leigh and Hull KR in their final two matches if they are to avoid missing out on the Super League play-offs for the first time.

Leeds Rhinos coach Brad Arthur told BBC Radio Leeds:

"I thought both our starts to the first half and the second half were pretty good. We did it with a good control.

"We had to stay composed and that was a good test for us. We had players all over the shop the last 15 minutes but they still had a pride in their defence which has been a bit questionable at times this season.

"If we can withstand the pressure for three, four sets, which we're going to have to do against Wigan next week, it can take a bit of confidence out of your opposition.

"We're up against a really good team who have been at the top of their game for a long, long time. So we're excited, we've done the work, now we've got to be confident."

Leeds: Miller; Hall, Bird, Handley, Newman; Croft, Connor; Oledzki, O'Connor, Jenkins, Watkins, Hankinson, Cassell.

Interchanges: Holroyd, Smith, Levi, Lodge.

Referee: Marcus Griffiths.
